Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with a finite-valued slope map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. The coefficient is a dimensionless formal amount; state labels retain their tags, so equal coefficients on different labels do not identify those labels. Compounds are equal exactly when their coefficient functions are equal.

For compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, define composition and nonnegative scaling pointwise by $(c+d)(x):=c(x)+d(x)$ and $(tc)(x):=t c(x)$. The zero function is the empty compound; in particular $0c=0$. Comparison axioms involving scaling still require a strictly positive scalar unless explicitly stated otherwise. The **mass** of $c$ is the finite sum $m(c):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)$. It is dimensionless bookkeeping mass, not thermodynamic mass or energy. The compound is positive when $m(c)>0$.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

The formula for mass is independent of the chosen finite set containing the support, and composition and scaling obey $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] proves these assertions.

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\mathsf{J}(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.
In the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$, the sequence $\epsilon_n:=1/(n+1)$, $n\in\mathbb N$, is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero.

derivations.claim: Suppose $A+C\prec B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. For each $k\in\mathbb N$, set $n=\sigma(k)$ and $r=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)>0$, and write $A/r=(1/r)A$. The embedding's successor rule and finite induction show that the sum of $n$ copies of $A/r$ is $r(A/r)=A$, and likewise for $B$. Scaling the given comparison by $1/r$ gives $A/r+C/r\prec B/r+C/r$. By composition consistency, replace the $n$ copies of $A/r$ one at a time by $B/r$, keeping the already replaced copies, the remaining copies, and $C/r$ as spectators; after these finitely many replacements, $A+\epsilon_k C\prec B+\epsilon_k C$. This holds for every natural index $k$. By [F3], $\epsilon_k>0$ and $\epsilon_k\to0$, so stability with $Z_0=Z_1=C$ gives $A\prec B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity implies $C=0$ and the conclusion is the premise itself. Conversely, $A\prec B$ gives $A+C\prec B+C$ by consistency.

For equal-total signed maps $u,v$, the difference $d=v-u$ has finite support and total coefficient zero, so $m(d^+)=m(d^-)$. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, their pointwise common part $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$ gives $u=k+d^-$ and $v=k+d^+$. Cancellation in step 1.1 proves $u\prec v$ exactly when $d^-\prec d^+$, which by [F2] is $u\preceq_s v$; adding a common signed map leaves $d$ unchanged by [F2].

If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, [F2] identifies these with comparisons of $(v-u)^-$ to $(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-$ to $(w-v)^+$. Consistency combines them. Their pointwise common minimum cancels by step 1.1, leaving $(w-u)^-\prec(w-u)^+$, which [F2] identifies as $u\preceq_s w$. The same finite-sum argument proves closure under addition; reflexivity follows from reflexivity of the zero compound.

By [A1] and $\beta>0$, every configuration satisfies
$0\le e^{-\beta U_N}\le e^{\beta BN}$, with the value $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$.
Fact [F7] makes the integrand and its restriction to $\Lambda_L^N$
measurable. For every simple minorant of this restricted integrand, [L1]
bounds its integral by the integral of the constant $e^{\beta BN}$ on
$\Lambda_L^N$.

The box and product-measure formulas [F2, F3] give
$\lambda_d^{\otimes N}(\Lambda_L^N)=L^{dN}$. Thus
$Z_{L,N}\le(ae^{\beta B}L^d)^N/N!=(QL^d)^N/N!$ for $N\ge1$, and this
also holds for $N=0$ since $Z_{L,0}=1$.

Summing the nonnegative terms by [F6] and using [F4] gives
$1\le\Xi_L\le\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}(QL^d)^N/N!=e^{QL^d}$; the lower bound is
the empty-configuration term.

By [F8], $KL^d<n_L\le KL^d+1$. If $N>n_L$, then $N>KL^d$, so
$1\le e^{N-KL^d}$. Therefore
$$\sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-KL^d}\sum_{N>n_L}\frac{(eQL^d)^N}{N!}\le e^{-KL^d}e^{eQL^d}=e^{(eQ-K)L^d}\le e^{-L^d}.$$
The second inequality extends a nonnegative partial tail to the full
exponential series; the equality uses [F5], and the last inequality follows
from $K>eQ+1$ and [F5].

For each $M>n_L$, split the $M$th partial sum into the fixed finite prefix
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}$ and the finite tail from $n_L+1$ through $M$.
Taking suprema over $M$ in the nonnegative-series definition [F6] gives
$\Xi_L=\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}+\sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}$; subtraction is valid because
step 3.1 proves $\Xi_L<\infty$. Since $\Xi_L\ge1$, step 3.2 implies
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge\Xi_L-e^{-L^d}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$, let $\phi$ be a stable pair
potential as in [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]] with
stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. In fixed reference length and
energy units, put $\Lambda_L=[0,L]^d$ and define, for $N\ge1$,
$$Z_{L,N}:=\frac{a^N}{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta U_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N},$$
where $\lambda_d$ is Lebesgue measure restricted to the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R^d$, $\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ is its $N$-fold product measure. The
integrand uses the ordinary real exponential when $U_N<+\infty$ and is defined
to be $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$. Also,
$\int_{\Lambda_L^N}f\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ abbreviates the nonnegative
integral of $f\mathbf1_{\Lambda_L^N}$ on the full product space, using
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. Set $Z_{L,0}=1$.
Define $\Xi_L:=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}Z_{L,N}$ as the nonnegative extended sum of
[[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. For $L\ge1$ put
$Q:=a e^{\beta B}$. Choose any real $K>eQ+1$ and set
$$n_L:=\lfloor K L^d\rfloor+1.$$
which satisfies $K L^d<n_L\le K L^d+1$ by the integer-part lemma
[[lem-integer-part]]. Let
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}:=\sum_{N=0}^{n_L}Z_{L,N}$. Then
$$1\le\Xi_L\le e^{Q L^d},\qquad \sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-L^d},\qquad \Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L.$$

integral of $f\mathbf1_{\Lambda_L^N}$ on the full product space, using
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. Set $Z_{L,0}=1$.
Define $\Xi_L:=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}Z_{L,N}$ as the nonnegative extended sum of
[[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. For $L\ge1$ put
$Q:=a e^{\beta B}$. Choose any real $K>eQ+1$ and set
$$n_L:=\lfloor K L^d\rfloor+1.$$
which satisfies $K L^d<n_L\le K L^d+1$ by the integer-part lemma
[[lem-integer-part]]. Let
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}:=\sum_{N=0}^{n_L}Z_{L,N}$. Then
$$1\le\Xi_L\le e^{Q L^d},\qquad \sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-L^d},\qquad \Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a positive integer $d$ and use the Euclidean space $\mathbb R^d$ with norm
$\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A
pair potential is an even Borel-measurable function
$\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ whose image is contained in
$\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. Here $\overline{\mathbb R}$ is the extended real
line ([[def-extended-reals]]). Borel measurability means the inverse image of
each Borel subset of $\overline{\mathbb R}$ belongs to the Borel sigma-algebra
generated by open sets in the Euclidean topology on $\mathbb R^d$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. The value
$+\infty$ represents a forbidden pair separation. Coordinates and
potential values are numerical values in fixed reference length and energy
units.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

derivations.claim: For $P\ll Q$ with density $h$, the negative part of $h\log h$ is integrable because $-u\log u\leq1/e$ for $0\leq u\leq1$; the density definition is therefore unambiguous. Also $u\log u\geq u-1$ for $u\geq0$, so $D(P\Vert Q)=\int h\log h\,dQ\geq\int(h-1)\,dQ=0$. If $P\not\ll Q$, the defined value is $+\infty\geq0$.

For bounded $\phi$, let $Q_\phi$ have density $e^\phi/Q(e^\phi)$ relative to $Q$. When $P\ll Q$ and $D(P\Vert Q)<\infty$, the density logarithm identity gives $D(P\Vert Q_\phi)=D(P\Vert Q)-P(\phi)+\log Q(e^\phi)\geq0$ by step 1.1. Thus every variational test is at most $D(P\Vert Q)$; the same upper bound is immediate if $D=+\infty$. If $P\not\ll Q$, choose a measurable $Q$-null set $N$ with $P(N)>0$ and use $\phi=t\mathbf1_N$: then $Q(e^\phi)=1$ and $P(\phi)=tP(N)\to\infty$.

In the remaining case $P\ll Q$, let $h=dP/dQ$ and set $\phi_m=\max(-m,\min(m,\log h))$, taking $\phi_m=-m$ on $\{h=0\}$. Then $e^{\phi_m}\to h$ and $e^{\phi_m}\leq1+h$, so [F4] gives $Q(e^{\phi_m})\to1$. The negative part of $h\phi_m$ is bounded by $1/e$, and its positive part increases to $(h\log h)^+$; hence [F4] gives $P(\phi_m)=\int h\phi_m\,dQ\to D(P\Vert Q)$, including when the positive entropy part is infinite. Combining this with step 2.1 proves the variational identity.

If $T$ is measurable, every bounded test $\psi$ on the target pulls back to the bounded test $\psi\circ T$ on the source, and $Q(e^{\psi\circ T})=(Q\circ T^{-1})(e^\psi)$ while $P(\psi\circ T)=(P\circ T^{-1})(\psi)$. Taking suprema in step 3.1 proves the restriction inequality.

Finiteness of $D(P_{S,Y}\Vert P_S\otimes Q_Y)$ gives a joint density and its conditional kernel by [F2]. Pushing forward by $(s,y)\mapsto(r(s),y)$ and using step 4.1 gives finite $D(P_{R,Y}\Vert P_R\otimes Q_Y)$, so [F2] supplies the corresponding conditional kernel for $R$ as well. Thus all conditional densities and references in this clause are defined. For a conditioning observation $R$, applying the variational identity pointwise to the conditional density $k_R(r,y)$ shows $$G(R)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(E_P\phi(R,Y)-E_P\!\left[\log\int e^{\phi(R,y)}Q_Y(dy)\right]\right),$$ where the tests range over bounded measurable functions of $(R,Y)$. The upper bound follows from step 2.1 for each conditional law; the reverse bound follows by using the jointly measurable bounded truncations of $\log k_R$ from step 3.1 and then [F3]–[F4]. When $R$ is a measurable function of $S$, every test depending on $(R,Y)$ is an admissible test depending on $(S,Y)$ with the same objective value, since the $Q_Y$ normalizer still depends only on $R$. Thus $G(R)\leq G(S)$; nonnegativity is step 1.1 applied conditionally.

Suppose $P_{XY}$ has density $h(x,y)$ relative to $Q_X\otimes Q_Y$. Put $h_X(x)=\int h(x,y)Q_Y(dy)$. By [F3], $h_X$ is a density for $P_X$. Where $0<h_X(x)<\infty$, [F2] supplies the conditional density $k(x,y)=h(x,y)/h_X(x)$ relative to $Q_Y$; elsewhere use its supplied filler. On the full $P_X$-measure set of finite positive $h_X$, $h=h_Xk$ and $\log h=\log h_X+\log k$ $P_{XY}$-almost everywhere. Integrating this identity, with nonnegative conditional entropies and finite total entropy, gives the displayed chain rule. If a restriction entropy is infinite, step 4.1 makes the joint entropy infinite as well, so no subtraction of two infinite terms is used.

Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 prove nonnegativity and the variational identity, step 4.1 proves restriction monotonicity, step 5.1 proves the product chain rule, and step 4.2 proves monotonicity under additional conditioning.

Assume AC. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on one measurable space and use $D(P\Vert Q)$ as defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. Then
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(P(\phi)-\log Q(e^\phi)\right),$$
where $B_b$ is the set of bounded real measurable functions. In particular $D\geq0$. If $T$ is measurable, then $D(P\circ T^{-1}\Vert Q\circ T^{-1})\leq D(P\Vert Q)$.

For standard-Borel spaces $X,Y$, probability reference measures $Q_X,Q_Y$, and a joint probability $P_{XY}\ll Q_X\otimes Q_Y$ with finite $D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)$, let $P_{Y|X=x}$ be the conditional law supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for nested standard-Borel observations $R$ and $S$ with $R$ a measurable function of $S$, and a fixed probability reference $Q_Y$ for a further variable $Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever the joint relative entropy is finite.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. The coefficient is a dimensionless formal amount; state labels retain their tags, so equal coefficients on different labels do not identify those labels. Compounds are equal exactly when their coefficient functions are equal.

For compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, define composition and nonnegative scaling pointwise by $(c+d)(x):=c(x)+d(x)$ and $(tc)(x):=t c(x)$. The zero function is the empty compound; in particular $0c=0$. Comparison axioms involving scaling still require a strictly positive scalar unless explicitly stated otherwise. The **mass** of $c$ is the finite sum $m(c):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)$. It is dimensionless bookkeeping mass, not thermodynamic mass or energy. The compound is positive when $m(c)>0$.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

The formula for mass is independent of the chosen finite set containing the support, and composition and scaling obey $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] proves these assertions.

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.
5. **Stability:** for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive compounds $Z_0,Z_1$ with $m(Z_0)=m(Z_1)$, and a sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to $0$, if $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\preceq B$.
6. **Comparison hypothesis (CH):** for every equal-mass pair $A,B$, either $A\preceq B$ or $B\preceq A$ (or both).

These are mathematical assumptions, not conclusions about a physical system. No antisymmetry, continuity, convexity, or strict comparison is included. Strict comparison means $A\preceq B$ and not $B\preceq A$.

Let $u,v:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite-support real coefficient maps with equal total coefficient $\sum_xu(x)=\sum_xv(x)$. These signed maps are formal comparison notation, not compounds. Put $d:=v-u$ and define $d^+(x):=\max\{d(x),0\}$ and $d^-(x):=\max\{-d(x),0\}$. Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.
In the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$, the sequence $\epsilon_n:=1/(n+1)$, $n\in\mathbb N$, is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero.

derivations.claim: For equal-total $u,v$, $d=v-u$ has finite support and total sum zero. Pointwise $d=d^+-d^-$, so finite-sum linearity gives $m(d^+)-m(d^-)=0$; both maps are finite-support and nonnegative. Thus the definition in [F2] compares equal-mass compounds. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, set $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$; then $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$.

Suppose $A+C\preceq B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. For each $k\in\mathbb N$, set $n=\sigma(k)$ and $r=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)>0$, and write $A/r=(1/r)A$. The embedding's successor rule and finite induction show that the sum of $n$ copies of $A/r$ is $r(A/r)=A$, and likewise for $B$. Scaling the given comparison by $1/r$ gives $A/r+C/r\preceq B/r+C/r$. By composition consistency, replace the $n$ copies of $A/r$ one at a time by $B/r$, keeping the already replaced copies, the remaining copies, and $C/r$ as spectators; after these finitely many replacements, $A+\epsilon_k C\preceq B+\epsilon_k C$. This holds for every natural index $k$. By [F3], $\epsilon_k>0$ and $\epsilon_k\to0$, so stability with $Z_0=Z_1=C$ gives $A\preceq B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity implies $C=0$ and the conclusion is the premise itself. Conversely, $A\preceq B$ gives $A+C\preceq B+C$ by consistency.

For nonnegative $u,v$, step 1.1 gives $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$. Cancellation from step 1.2 shows $u\preceq v$ exactly when $(v-u)^-\preceq(v-u)^+$, which is $u\preceq_s v$. For general signed maps, adding a common map leaves $v-u$ unchanged, so it leaves signed comparison unchanged.

If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, then consistency combines $(v-u)^-\preceq(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-\preceq(w-v)^+$ into a comparison between the sums of their negative and positive parts. The two sums have a common pointwise minimum; cancel it by step 1.2. The remaining maps are precisely $(w-u)^-$ and $(w-u)^+$, so $u\preceq_s w$. The same sum-and-cancel argument applied to two independent signed comparisons proves closure under their addition; reflexivity follows from $0\preceq0$.

Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

For $g>2R_0$ set
$$\eta(g)=g^d\psi(g)+\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr.$$
Then $\eta(g)\to0$ and
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Moreover, there is a choice $g(\ell)>0$, for all sufficiently large real $\ell$, such that $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and
$$\left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\longrightarrow0.$$
For every fixed finite configuration and all sufficiently large periods $L$, the noncoincident periodic-image tail $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d,\ |k|_\infty\geq K_0}|\phi(x-y+Lk)|$ is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim: Write $N_i=N_{C_i}(\omega)$. The negative part of each pair potential is bounded both by $2B$, where $B$ is the stability constant of $\phi$, and, at large separation, by the lower-regular envelope. Set $\Psi_j$ to a finite constant on the finitely many near-cell offsets and to the envelope evaluated at $|j|_\infty-1$ on the remaining offsets. The shell count $|\{j:|j|_\infty=m\}|\leq c_dm^{d-1}$ and the cell-envelope conclusion of [F2] give $\sum_j\Psi_j<\infty$. Since $N_iN_j\leq(N_i^2+N_j^2)/2$, the total negative pair contribution is at most $C\sum_iN_i^2$ for a finite $C$.

In case (i), choose an integer $k_0\geq2$ with $1/(k_0-1)\leq r_1$. Then $\chi(1/k)$ and $\chi(1/(k-1))$ are both defined for every $k\geq k_0$. Partition one unit cell into $k^d$ half-open cubes of side $1/k$, put $\chi_k=\chi(1/k)$, and $\Delta\chi_k=\chi_k-\chi_{k-1}\geq0$. If the cell contains $N$ points, the identity $\sum_jn_j^2-N=2\sum_j\binom{n_j}{2}$ and nonnegativity of $\sum_j(n_j-N/k^d)^2$ give at least $\frac12(N^2/k^d-N)$ same-subcube pairs at scale $k$. A fixed pair counted at scale $k$ has separation $s<1/k$, hence $k<1/s$; summing its nonnegative weights over all scales where it is counted is at most $\sum_{k=k_0}^{\lfloor1/s\rfloor}\Delta\chi_k\leq\chi(s)$. Thus the positive core energy in the cell dominates the sum of these weighted pair counts. With $K_N=\lfloor(N/2)^{1/d}\rfloor$, each $k\leq K_N$ satisfies $N^2/k^d-N\geq N^2/(2k^d)$, so the core energy is at least $$ \frac{N^2}{4}\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N}\frac{\Delta\chi_k}{k^d}. $$ Summation by parts writes the coefficient as an initial constant plus $\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N-1}\chi_k(k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d})$; and $k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d}\geq d/(2^{d+1}k^{d+1})$. The series $\sum_k\chi(1/k)k^{-d-1}$ diverges: on dyadic intervals $[2^{-j-1},2^{-j}]$, monotonicity bounds the integral above by $C_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$, while the corresponding block $2^{j+1}\leq k<2^{j+2}$ contributes at least $c_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$ to that series. The divergent core integral therefore forces the displayed coefficient to tend to infinity.

In case (i), sum the cell core bound from step 1.2 and subtract the negative-pair bound from step 1.1. The resulting coefficient of $N_i^2$ tends to infinity with $N_i$. Above a finite threshold it dominates $2CN_i^2$; below that threshold its possible negative remainder is bounded by a constant times $N_i$. Taking $h(N)$ to be half the positive cell lower bound above the threshold and zero below it gives a nondecreasing extended-valued function with $h(N)/N^2\to\infty$ and $H_\phi\geq\sum_i h(N_i)-bN$.

In case (ii), choose $k$ with $1/k<r_h$ and partition every unit cell into $k^d$ subcubes. A finite-energy configuration has at most one point in each subcube, so $N_i\leq k^d$ for every $i$. Define $h(N)=0$ for $N\leq k^d$ and $h(N)=+\infty$ for $N>k^d$. If any cell exceeds this occupancy, the configuration has a forbidden pair and $H_\phi=+\infty$; otherwise stability gives $H_\phi\geq-BN=\sum_i h(N_i)-BN$. This proves the hard-core alternative.

boundaries.evidence: Statement h(0)=0 and the empty configuration has H_0=0, making its energy estimate exact. The limit h(N)/N^2 concerns N tending to infinity, not evaluation of 0/0.

Assume the potential of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] is stable and regular. In addition, assume either (i) $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ is finite-valued and nonincreasing, $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$, and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; or (ii) there is a hard-core radius $r_h>0$ such that $\phi(x)=+\infty$ whenever $|x|_\infty<r_h$. Let $C$ be the open positive-temperature domain of a local C2 energy representation $\mathcal U_c(s,V,n)$ for a fixed material constitution $c$, with $V>0$, $n_j>0$, and conjugates $T=\mathcal U_{c,s}$, $p=-\mathcal U_{c,V}$, and $\mu_j=\mathcal U_{c,n_j}$. Let $W\subseteq C$ be open. In addition to the framework suppliers, assume the **same-tag homogeneity hypothesis**: for every $q=(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in W$ there is an $\varepsilon_q\in(0,1)$ such that

$$\mathcal U_c(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n_1,\ldots,\lambda n_r)=\lambda\mathcal U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$$

for every $\lambda>0$ with $|\lambda-1|<\varepsilon_q$ and $\lambda q\in C$. Then, throughout $W$,

$$\mathcal U_c=Ts-pV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j,$$

and on the same chart

$$s\,dT-V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j=0.$$

The same-tag hypothesis is supplied, in particular, when the inverse states $\Psi(q):=(\mathcal U_c(q),V,n)$ for $q\in W$ lie in the designated common-law cone of [[post-td-common-bulk-constitutive-law]], expressed in physical SI coordinate values using the fixed unit conversion. On this branch the adopted entropy transport implies the energy homogeneity locally by uniqueness of the local inverse; no global inverse or global energy-domain cone is assumed. These are conditional model deductions. The general tagged relation in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] alone does not identify the scaled system with one fixed constitutive law.

Let $P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P)$ be an admitted closed process record as defined in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$. The record is **reversible relative to its declared boundary and protocol** when the model also admits a reverse record $P^{\mathrm{rev}}$ for the same system and material constitution, starting at $x_P^+$ and ending at $x_P^-$, such that every auxiliary and device state specified by the protocol is restored to its initial state and every signed boundary transfer is reversed. In particular,

$$Q[P^{\mathrm{rev}}]=-Q[P],\qquad W_{\mathrm{on}}[P^{\mathrm{rev}}]=-W_{\mathrm{on}}[P].$$

If the protocol records additional transfer channels, their signed values must likewise be negatives of their forward values. A record that is slow is not reversible merely because it is slow; it must satisfy the reverse-record condition above. Reversibility is therefore relative to what the model includes inside the boundary and which reverse controls it admits.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound, and restrict to constituent splits for which [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] supplies the additive total entropy. The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^+)-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^-)\ge0,$$

where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the sum of the constituent entropies in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt zero total entropy change. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.

On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Let $C$ be the open positive-temperature domain of a local C2 energy representation $\mathcal U_c(s,V,n)$ for a fixed material constitution $c$, with $V>0$, $n_j>0$, and conjugates $T=\mathcal U_{c,s}$, $p=-\mathcal U_{c,V}$, and $\mu_j=\mathcal U_{c,n_j}$. Let $W\subseteq C$ be open. In addition to the framework suppliers, assume the **same-tag homogeneity hypothesis**: for every $q=(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in W$ there is an $\varepsilon_q\in(0,1)$ such that

$$\mathcal U_c(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n_1,\ldots,\lambda n_r)=\lambda\mathcal U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$$

for every $\lambda>0$ with $|\lambda-1|<\varepsilon_q$ and $\lambda q\in C$. Then, throughout $W$,

$$\mathcal U_c=Ts-pV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j,$$

and on the same chart

$$s\,dT-V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j=0.$$

The same-tag hypothesis is supplied, in particular, when the inverse states $\Psi(q):=(\mathcal U_c(q),V,n)$ for $q\in W$ lie in the designated common-law cone of [[post-td-common-bulk-constitutive-law]], expressed in physical SI coordinate values using the fixed unit conversion. On this branch the adopted entropy transport implies the energy homogeneity locally by uniqueness of the local inverse; no global inverse or global energy-domain cone is assumed. These are conditional model deductions. The general tagged relation in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] alone does not identify the scaled system with one fixed constitutive law.

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: By [F3], bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange give common $T_0,p_0$ and $\mu_\alpha=\mu_\beta$ at the attained interior coexistence point. Apply [F5] separately to the two phase branches using [A1]: $G_i/n_i=\mu_i$ for $i=\alpha,\beta$. Thus $F(T_0,p_0):=g_\beta(T_0,p_0)-g_\alpha(T_0,p_0)=0$.

On each branch, hold the amount $n_i$ fixed while varying $(T,p)$. By [F2] and [F4], $d(G_i/n_i)=-s_i\,dT+v_i\,dp$. Consequently $F_T=-(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$ and $F_p=v_\beta-v_\alpha$ at $(T_0,p_0)$. The nonzero-volume-jump hypothesis makes $F_p\ne0$.

Apply [L1] to $F=g_\beta-g_\alpha$ on $O$. It gives a unique local C1 graph $p=p(T)$ satisfying $F(T,p(T))=0$. Differentiating this identity using [L2] gives $0=F_T+F_p\,p'(T)$. Substitution of the derivatives from step 1.2 yields
$$
p'(T_0)=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
The same calculation applies at every point of the shrunken coexistence interval with nonzero $\Delta v$.

For the reversible latent-heat clause, the system entropy change when $n$ moles are converted is $n(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. By [A2], the full isolated compound has zero total entropy change; all other components have zero entropy change, and the reservoir contributes $-Q/T$, so $Q/T=n(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. Dividing by $n>0$ gives $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}:=Q/n=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. This conclusion is conditional on the stated reversible operation and ideal reservoir; it is not a property of an arbitrary irreversible conversion path.

Let $\alpha,\beta$ be two one-component phase branches from [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] on a common open chart $O\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(T,p)$. Assume each branch has a local $C^2$ energy representation $\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)$, $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, and that within each fixed branch tag it satisfies the same-tag homogeneity
$$
\mathcal U_i(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)
$$
for all $\lambda$ in a neighborhood of $1$ for which the scaled state remains in the chart. This is a phase-branch hypothesis: the general tagged law of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] does not imply it. It may be stipulated independently on each local branch, or supplied by the common-law bulk subclass of [[pthm-td-euler-and-gibbs-duhem]] when each phase's local inverse states lie in its designated entropy cone with fixed species and intensive parameters and common SI units and energy/entropy reference conventions. That supplied subclass uses local inverse uniqueness and does not require a global energy inverse.

Suppose a state $(T_0,p_0)\in O$ is an attained interior coexistence equilibrium with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange between the two branches, and both branches admit the valid local Gibbs charts of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Write $g_i=G_i/n_i$, $s_i=S_i/n_i$, and $v_i=V_i/n_i$ in the units specified by [[def-td-si-quantities]]. If
$$
\Delta v(T_0,p_0):=v_\beta(T_0,p_0)-v_\alpha(T_0,p_0)\ne0,
$$
then, on some open interval about $T_0$, the equal-Gibbs-per-mole coexistence condition $g_\alpha(T,p(T))=g_\beta(T,p(T))$ defines a unique local $C^1$ curve and
$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
If, in addition, conversion from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ is admitted as a reversible process in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at the same fixed $T$, then its molar latent heat absorbed by the system is $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. These are conditional model deductions. The slope conclusion is not asserted when $\Delta v=0$ or where the branch charts are not $C^1$.

Let $\alpha,\beta$ be two one-component phase branches from [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] on a common open chart $O\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(T,p)$. Assume each branch has a local $C^2$ energy representation $\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)$, $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, and that within each fixed branch tag it satisfies the same-tag homogeneity
$$
\mathcal U_i(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)
$$
for all $\lambda$ in a neighborhood of $1$ for which the scaled state remains in the chart. This is a phase-branch hypothesis: the general tagged law of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] does not imply it. It may be stipulated independently on each local branch, or supplied by the common-law bulk subclass of [[pthm-td-euler-and-gibbs-duhem]] when each phase's local inverse states lie in its designated entropy cone with fixed species and intensive parameters and common SI units and energy/entropy reference conventions. That supplied subclass uses local inverse uniqueness and does not require a global energy inverse.

Suppose a state $(T_0,p_0)\in O$ is an attained interior coexistence equilibrium with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange between the two branches, and both branches admit the valid local Gibbs charts of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Write $g_i=G_i/n_i$, $s_i=S_i/n_i$, and $v_i=V_i/n_i$ in the units specified by [[def-td-si-quantities]]. If
$$
\Delta v(T_0,p_0):=v_\beta(T_0,p_0)-v_\alpha(T_0,p_0)\ne0,
$$
then, on some open interval about $T_0$, the equal-Gibbs-per-mole coexistence condition $g_\alpha(T,p(T))=g_\beta(T,p(T))$ defines a unique local $C^1$ curve and
$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
If, in addition, conversion from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ is admitted as a reversible process in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at the same fixed $T$, then its molar latent heat absorbed by the system is $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. These are conditional model deductions. The slope conclusion is not asserted when $\Delta v=0$ or where the branch charts are not $C^1$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P)$ be an admitted closed process record as defined in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$. The record is **reversible relative to its declared boundary and protocol** when the model also admits a reverse record $P^{\mathrm{rev}}$ for the same system and material constitution, starting at $x_P^+$ and ending at $x_P^-$, such that every auxiliary and device state specified by the protocol is restored to its initial state and every signed boundary transfer is reversed. In particular,

$$Q[P^{\mathrm{rev}}]=-Q[P],\qquad W_{\mathrm{on}}[P^{\mathrm{rev}}]=-W_{\mathrm{on}}[P].$$

If the protocol records additional transfer channels, their signed values must likewise be negatives of their forward values. A record that is slow is not reversible merely because it is slow; it must satisfy the reverse-record condition above. Reversibility is therefore relative to what the model includes inside the boundary and which reverse controls it admits.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound, and restrict to constituent splits for which [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] supplies the additive total entropy. The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^+)-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^-)\ge0,$$

where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the sum of the constituent entropies in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt zero total entropy change. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous.
