supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. No differentiability, strict concavity, or positive $S_U$ is asserted outside those charts. This item does not itself define a thermometer calibration or claim a temperature law.

For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. Lieb–Yngvason develop a different accessibility-based route in which entropy is represented from additional operational hypotheses; this framework does not claim that their derivation proves the present primitive entropy postulate.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a material constitution $c$ and its equilibrium state domain $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Let $\Omega\subseteq D_c$ be a specified open, single-phase chart in physical SI coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, with $U$ evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. On $\Omega$, use the finite $C^2$ entropy function $S_c$ and the strict positivity $S_{c,U}>0$ adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Here $C^2$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in that coordinate direction while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Define the **absolute thermodynamic temperature**, **entropic pressure**, and **molar chemical potential** of species $j$ by

$$T_c:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}},\qquad p_c:=T_cS_{c,V},\qquad \mu_{c,j}:=-T_cS_{c,n_j}.$$

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq 1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$, and a bounded measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$, write $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above. A periodic model uses the declared periodic cell and sums its periodic-image pair interactions with each unordered pair counted once. These are distinct boundary preparations. The limits on this page are positional configurational limits and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

Use the periodic boxes $\Lambda_n$ and positional energy of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]], and the exact-$N$ measure $\mu_{\Lambda_n,N}$ of [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]]. Given $N_n\in\mathbb N$, a reduced configuration-energy center $e\in\mathbb R$ joules per dimensionless reference volume, and a width $\delta_n>0$ in the same units, define
$$S_n(N_n,e,\delta_n)=\{\omega\subset\Lambda_n:|\omega|=N_n,\ |H_{N_n}^{\mathrm{per}}(\omega)/V_n-e|\leq\delta_n\}.$$
When $0<\mu_{\Lambda_n,N_n}(S_n)<\infty$, the uniform positional shell law is
$$M_n(A)=\frac{\mu_{\Lambda_n,N_n}(A\cap S_n)}{\mu_{\Lambda_n,N_n}(S_n)}.$$
A shrinking energy-density shell uses some specified sequence $\delta_n\downarrow0$. Its total energy width is $2\delta_nV_n$, which is $o(V_n)$ but need not be microscopic or bounded. Existence of a normalizing shell and the existence of a suitable shrinking sequence are separate theorem obligations. This is not a surface measure on an exact-energy hypersurface and not a phase-space shell for $K(p)+H_N^{\mathrm{per}}$.

For a specified finite region and boundary preparation, take $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and the positional energy in [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. For each fixed $N$, specialize the measurable-model canonical preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] to the dimensionless positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$; adopt the law
$$P_{\Lambda,N}^{\mathrm{can}}(d\omega)=Z_{\Lambda,N}^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega),\qquad Z_{\Lambda,N}=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\mu_{\Lambda,N},$$
whenever $0<Z_{\Lambda,N}<\infty$. Separately adopt the grand-canonical law at activity $z>0$ to have weights $z^{N(\omega)}e^{-\beta H_{N(\omega)}(\omega)}$ relative to the same indistinguishable positional measures; its normalizer is $\Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda,N}$ when finite. Here $z$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity in [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]], and $\alpha=\log z$.

For the controlled positional shell of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]], adopt the conditional measure $M_n$ only when its shell has positive finite reference measure. These are probability-law preparations used to define the model. They are not derived from Hamiltonian trajectories, and they do not assert that a laboratory apparatus reaches any of them. The inverse-temperature-zero hard-core continuation is governed separately by [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]].

Fix the selected stable regularly tempered pair model with Borel-measurable $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$, $T>0$, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ with the SI conventions of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]], and activity $z>0$. For the superstable branch, require measurable even pair potentials $\varphi_s,\varphi_r$ with $\varphi=\varphi_s+\varphi_r$, where $\varphi_s$ is stable in joules and $\varphi_r(x)\geq0$ joules for every $x$. Require constants $\epsilon>0$ joules and $r_0>0$ in dimensionless coordinates such that $\varphi_r(x)\geq\epsilon$ whenever $\|x\|_\infty\leq r_0$, where $\|x\|_\infty=\max_j|x_j|$. These are exactly the stable-plus-nonnegative-core conditions of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] for $\widehat\varphi$, after energy conversion; this is an additional model hypothesis, not a consequence of stability alone.

Under the Axiom of Choice, use the global measurable configuration space $\Omega$ of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], consisting of locally finite simple configurations with sigma-algebra generated by bounded-Borel count maps. For $a\in\mathbb R^d$, let $T_a\omega(A)=\omega(A-a)$ be its measurable translation. A probability law $P$ on $\Omega$ is stationary exactly when $P\circ T_a^{-1}=P$ for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$. For a bounded Borel region $A$, equip its finite simple configuration set $\mathcal C_A$ with $\mathcal F_A^{\rm count}=\sigma(N_B:B\subseteq A\text{ Borel})$, without completing it. On this space $r_A(\omega)=\omega\cap A$ is measurable: each generating count satisfies $N_B\circ r_A=N_B$, a bounded-Borel global count. Write $P_A=P\circ r_A^{-1}$ on this exact count sigma-algebra for every stationary $P$. This assertion does not extend $P_A$ to the completed quotient sigma-algebra. The reference $Q_A=Q\circ r_A^{-1}$ is the restriction of the same unit-intensity law $Q$; by [[thm-tdmath-poisson-reference-count-properties]] and the count-generated restriction sigma-algebra, it equals the restriction to $\mathcal F_A^{\rm count}$ of the finite-sector law $e^{-|A|}\sum_{N\geq0}\mu_{A,N}$ of [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]]. This count sigma-algebra is contained in the completed quotient sigma-algebra: in each sector, the pullback of $N_B$ is $\sum_{j=1}^N\mathbf1_B(x_j)$, a Borel function, so each count generator is quotient measurable. Thus the stated restriction of the positional measure is defined. Relative entropy and the restrictions below always use $\mathcal F_A^{\rm count}$, exactly as in the mathematical global supplier, rather than an unproved completion for arbitrary $P$. Indeed, a finite Borel partition of $A$ has multinomial counts under each fixed-$N$ Lebesgue sector, and summing these sector measures with the factor $e^{-|A|}$ gives independent Poisson counts of the corresponding volumes. Use the finite-region relative entropy $D(P_0\|Q_0)$ of [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]: if $P_0\ll Q_0$ and $h=dP_0/dQ_0$, then $D=\int h\log h\,dQ_0$ with $0\log0=0$; otherwise $D=+\infty$. Let $C=[-1/2,1/2)^d$ and define $\rho(P)=E_PN_C$. On stationary laws for which the finite limits exist, define
$$I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{D(P_{\Lambda_L}\|Q_{\Lambda_L})}{|\Lambda_L|},\qquad \Phi(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{E_P[H_{\Lambda_L}^{\mathrm{free}}]}{|\Lambda_L|}.$$
For $\beta>0$, use the stationary laws with finite $I(P)$ and $\Phi(P)$ and adopt, at the selected $(\varphi,\beta,z)$, that
$$\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{P}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}=\{P^\ast\}.$$

For the $\beta=0$ branch, require a nonempty hard-core displacement set $B=\{x:\varphi(x)=+\infty\}$ and use [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]]. A global configuration is hard-admissible when no pair of its distinct points has displacement in $B$. Restrict to stationary laws assigning probability one to hard-admissible configurations and having finite $I(P)$; adopt, at the selected $z$, that
$$\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{P}\{I(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}=\{P^\ast\}.$$

A finite configuration is a finite subset $\omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with no repeated points; its number of points is $N(\omega)$. A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. $$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. $$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$

Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq 1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$, and a bounded measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$, write $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above. A periodic model uses the declared periodic cell and sums its periodic-image pair interactions with each unordered pair counted once. These are distinct boundary preparations. The limits on this page are positional configurational limits and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

Use the dimensionless coordinates, simple configurations, and pair potential of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. A sequence $(\Lambda_k)_{k\geq1}$ of bounded measurable regions is van Hove if $|\Lambda_k|\to\infty$ and, for every fixed $s>0$,
$$\frac{|\{x\in\Lambda_k:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Lambda_k)\leq s\}|}{|\Lambda_k|}\longrightarrow0.$$
This is an explicit condition on the boundary-layer volume; increasing volume alone does not imply it. A free wall permits particles only in $\Lambda_k$ and includes no exterior particles. A periodic wall uses the specified periodic cell and its image convention.

For the deterministic exterior class, let $C=[-1/2,1/2)^d$ and $\Lambda_n=[-n-1/2,n+1/2)^d$, with $V_n=|\Lambda_n|$. For a locally finite exterior configuration $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$, write $N_{C+i}(\zeta)=|\zeta\cap(C+i)|$. Given $t<\infty$, define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C+i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\ \text{for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For an interior configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_n$, its exterior interaction is
$$W_n(\omega,\zeta)=\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n}\varphi(x-y),$$
interpreted as an extended-real sum. A positive infinite value has zero Boltzmann weight. The regular tail controls distant terms; the class $\Omega(t)$ is a fixed uniform bound on exterior cell counts, not permission for an arbitrary volume-filling external potential. The van Hove and uniformly tempered exterior conditions are separate boundary regimes.

For a specified finite region and boundary preparation, take $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and the positional energy in [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. For each fixed $N$, specialize the measurable-model canonical preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] to the dimensionless positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$; adopt the law
$$P_{\Lambda,N}^{\mathrm{can}}(d\omega)=Z_{\Lambda,N}^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega),\qquad Z_{\Lambda,N}=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\mu_{\Lambda,N},$$
whenever $0<Z_{\Lambda,N}<\infty$. Separately adopt the grand-canonical law at activity $z>0$ to have weights $z^{N(\omega)}e^{-\beta H_{N(\omega)}(\omega)}$ relative to the same indistinguishable positional measures; its normalizer is $\Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda,N}$ when finite. Here $z$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity in [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]], and $\alpha=\log z$.

For the controlled positional shell of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]], adopt the conditional measure $M_n$ only when its shell has positive finite reference measure. These are probability-law preparations used to define the model. They are not derived from Hamiltonian trajectories, and they do not assert that a laboratory apparatus reaches any of them. The inverse-temperature-zero hard-core continuation is governed separately by [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]].

Assume AC. Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$, use the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|_2$ from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define $|x|_\infty=\max_j|x_j|$, and use the numerical coordinate conventions in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. A finite configuration is a finite subset $\omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with no repeated points; its number of points is $N(\omega)$. A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$. These are the conventions used for the interacting results on this page. A genuine divergent positive core is the separate additional condition that some nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$ and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; it is not implied by superstability.

For $L>0$ put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $V_L=L^d$, and let $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ be $H_\phi$ for configurations restricted to $\Lambda_L$. For sufficiently large periodic cubes, periodize $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ by $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and set
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x}\phi(y-x),$$
interpreting the value as $+\infty$ if a positive infinite term occurs. The far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below. With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$. The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$. A physical pressure identification is not part of this mathematical definition.

For a stationary probability law $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$. When the limit exists, write
$$\mathcal E(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}E_PH_{L,\mathrm{free}},\qquad I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
The cited results below establish existence under their stated hypotheses; this definition does not assume it for every stationary law.

Assume a superstable regular pair potential $\phi$ as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and the van Hove definition [[def-tdmath-van-hove-sequence]]. For a bounded Lebesgue-measurable $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$, define $\mathcal S_N(\Lambda)=\{(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\Lambda^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ and $H_N(q)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)$. With $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, set
$$Z_\Lambda(N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda)}e^{-\beta H_N(q)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_\Lambda(0;\beta)=1,\qquad \Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_\Lambda(N;\beta).$$
This is the labelled positional Lebesgue integral with indistinguishable-particle normalization and includes no exterior interaction. For $\Lambda=[0,L)^d$ it agrees with $Z(L,N;\beta)$ and $\Xi(L;z,\beta)$ from [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. For every van Hove sequence $(\Omega_k)$ and fixed $z,\beta>0$, the free-wall grand pressure satisfies
$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac1{|\Omega_k|}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)=p(z,\beta),$$
where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube limit from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The extra superstability hypothesis supplies the uniform cell-occupation bound used below; no arbitrary-shape theorem under stability alone is claimed.

Assume superstability and regularity, let $(\Omega_k)$ be van Hove, and let $N_k/|\Omega_k|\to\rho$ for an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. Use the general-region free-wall convention of [[thm-tdmath-superstable-van-hove-pressure]], namely
$$Z(\Lambda,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\{q\in\Lambda^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}}\exp\!\left(-\beta\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)\right)dq_1\cdots dq_N\quad(N\geq1),$$
with $Z(\Lambda,0;\beta)=1$ and $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, for bounded Lebesgue-measurable $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$. For the free-wall exact-$N_k$ positional partition with this $1/N_k!$ normalization,
$$|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log Z(\Omega_k,N_k;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho),$$
the free-cube canonical rate of [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]. Superstability is used for the arbitrary-shape pressure upper bound; no stability-only upper theorem is asserted.

Assume a stable regular pair potential $\phi$ as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and the genuine finite-valued positive-core condition of [[lem-tdmath-superquadratic-positive-core]]: for some $r_0>0$, a nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_0]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_0$ and $\int_0^{r_0}\chi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr=+\infty$. Let $\Lambda_n=[-n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)^d$, $V_n=(2n+1)^d$, $C_i=i+[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)^d$, and $\mathcal C_{\rm lf}$ be the set of locally finite simple configurations $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$. For $t\geq0$ define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta\in\mathcal C_{\rm lf}:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\text{ for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$

$$H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)=H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)+\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{y\in\zeta_n^{\rm out}}\phi(q_i-y).$$
The exterior series has finite negative part by the proof below; its extended value may be $+\infty$, with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$. Define
$$Z_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_{n,\zeta}(0;\beta)=1,\qquad \Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta).$$
For fixed $z,\beta>0$ and $t<\infty$, the free-wall grand pressure with this exterior pair energy satisfies
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\zeta\in\Omega(t)}\left|\frac1{V_n}\log\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)-p(z,\beta)\right|=0,$$
where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube pressure from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The exterior configuration is restricted to the stated fixed square-count class; no volume-filling external field is included. The conclusion is conditional on the genuine positive core and does not infer it from superstability alone.

derivations.claim: Under the Borel superstable regular hypotheses of [L0] and the physical pair assumptions [F1], the finite-dimensional norm bounds in [F2] transfer the local van Hove sequence to the supplier's $\ell^\infty$ boundary convention. citations.quote:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

Let $\mathcal F$ be the explicitly declared feasible endpoint set of an isolated compound whose constituents are independent separated macroscopic systems, as defined in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. For this route, adopt the physical criterion that any endpoint tuple the model classifies as a stable equilibrium under these fixed totals, retained partitions, and permitted exchanges satisfies

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a material constitution $c$ and its equilibrium state domain $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Let $\Omega\subseteq D_c$ be a specified open, single-phase chart in physical SI coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, with $U$ evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. On $\Omega$, use the finite $C^2$ entropy function $S_c$ and the strict positivity $S_{c,U}>0$ adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Here $C^2$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in that coordinate direction while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Define the **absolute thermodynamic temperature**, **entropic pressure**, and **molar chemical potential** of species $j$ by

$$T_c:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}},\qquad p_c:=T_cS_{c,V},\qquad \mu_{c,j}:=-T_cS_{c,n_j}.$$

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq 1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$, and a bounded measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$, write $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above. A periodic model uses the declared periodic cell and sums its periodic-image pair interactions with each unordered pair counted once. These are distinct boundary preparations. The limits on this page are positional configurational limits and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

For a specified finite region and boundary preparation, take $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and the positional energy in [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. For each fixed $N$, specialize the measurable-model canonical preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] to the dimensionless positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$; adopt the law
$$P_{\Lambda,N}^{\mathrm{can}}(d\omega)=Z_{\Lambda,N}^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega),\qquad Z_{\Lambda,N}=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\mu_{\Lambda,N},$$
whenever $0<Z_{\Lambda,N}<\infty$. Separately adopt the grand-canonical law at activity $z>0$ to have weights $z^{N(\omega)}e^{-\beta H_{N(\omega)}(\omega)}$ relative to the same indistinguishable positional measures; its normalizer is $\Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda,N}$ when finite. Here $z$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity in [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]], and $\alpha=\log z$.

For the controlled positional shell of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]], adopt the conditional measure $M_n$ only when its shell has positive finite reference measure. These are probability-law preparations used to define the model. They are not derived from Hamiltonian trajectories, and they do not assert that a laboratory apparatus reaches any of them. The inverse-temperature-zero hard-core continuation is governed separately by [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]].

Let $F_\beta$ be the finite concave canonical rate on the interior attainable-density interval from [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]. Extend it by $F_\beta(0)=0$, by its interior upper-semicontinuous limit at any finite upper endpoint of its effective domain, and by $-\infty$ outside the closed effective domain; retain the value $-\infty$ if the endpoint limit is $-\infty$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$. These are thermodynamic limits of positional partition functions. They do not assert local-observable equivalence, a finite-volume endpoint realization, or a thin energy-shell limit.

derivations.claim: By [A1], the physical positional partition sum is $\Xi_L(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda_L,N}$. Set $\alpha=\log z$; then $z^N=e^{\alpha N}$. Translate the centered cube by $L/2$ in each coordinate to $[0,L)^d$; this preserves Lebesgue measure and every pair displacement, so the positional partition is exactly the free-cube sum of [L1]. The dimensionless energy conversion in [F1] matches its numerical $\widehat\beta$.

The conditional conclusion of [L1] gives a finite limit $P(\log z,\widehat\beta)$ for $|\Lambda_L|^{-1}\log\Xi_L$. Multiplying by $k_BT/\ell_0^d$, which is independent of $L$, converts the dimensionless reference-volume rate to pressure per physical volume.

The vacuum term gives $b(0)=0$: $Z(L,0)=1$ is a lower bound, and the same stability estimate with $N/L^d\to0$ gives a nonpositive upper limit.

The effective domain of $F$ has nonempty interior. Fix a core cube of side $s>0$ and a gap $g>2R_0$; place one particle in each selected core of a lattice of spacing $s+g$ inside a large box. The absolute interaction from any one occupied core to all others is bounded by $C\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2], with the gap satisfying the stated hypothesis of the diagonal-gap estimate. Restricting each particle to a subcube of volume $v_0>0$ therefore gives $Z(L,N;\beta)\geq v_0^N e^{-C_0N}$ for every density strictly below $(s+g)^{-d}$, after omitting unused lattice cells. Thus $F$ is finite on a nonempty interval of positive densities; by its definition as a finite-mixture envelope it is concave.

Choose $W$ large enough to contain at least $C_1L^{d-1}$ small cells separated from each other and every core by more than $R_0$. Put each missing particle in one such cell. By the definition of $b$, every sequence with density tending $\rho$ has limsup rate at most $b(\rho)\leq F(\rho)$. Together with step 4.1 this proves the asserted limit. $$b(\rho)=\sup\left\{\limsup_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta):\frac{N_j}{L_j^d}\to\rho\right\}.$$
Let $F$ be the concave envelope of $b$ on $[0,\infty)$, namely the supremum of $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i b(\rho_i)$ over finite lists with $\theta_i\geq0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, $\rho_i\geq0$, and $\sum_i\theta_i\rho_i=\rho$; the empty supremum is $-\infty$. On the interior of $\{\rho:F(\rho)>-\infty\}$, $F$ is finite and continuous. For every $\rho>0$ in that interior and every such sequence $(L_j,N_j)$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$
No claim is made at a close-packing endpoint or at any other excluded endpoint.

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.
Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable. Then $\int\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu$.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

The metric space $\mathbb C$ is complete. A sequence $z_n=x_n+iy_n$ converges to $x+iy$ exactly when $x_n\to x$ and $y_n\to y$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]], [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]].

derivations.claim: The set on which $(f_n)$ is Cauchy is measurable: write it as the countable intersection/union/intersection of sets $\{|f_n-f_k|<1/m\}$ using [F4]. On this set the finite real and imaginary limits exist; their measurable limit functions, set to zero on its complement, define the measurable $f_0$. The assumed almost-everywhere convergence gives $f_0=f$ outside a measurable null set. Enlarge that set by the countably many measurable domination exceptions to a measurable null set $N$. Set $f_n$ and $f_0$ to zero on $N$, which preserves their measurability. A nonnegative measurable function supported on $N$ has integral zero by the simple-minorant definition, so these changes preserve every defined integral. Convergence and domination now hold everywhere, and $|f_0|\le g$ proves integrability. This does not redefine the potentially nonmeasurable $f$ and then claim it was measurable.

First take all functions real. The nonnegative functions $f_n+g$ converge pointwise to $f_0+g$. Fatou gives $\int(f_0+g)\le\liminf_n\int(f_n+g)=\int g+\liminf_n\int f_n$, so $\int f_0\le\liminf_n\int f_n$. Applying Fatou to $g-f_n\ge0$ gives $\int(g-f_0)\le\liminf_n\int(g-f_n)=\int g-\limsup_n\int f_n$, hence $\limsup_n\int f_n\le\int f_0$. Additivity of integrable signed integrals follows by writing each as a difference of its positive and negative parts and using [F3]. The inequalities imply convergence of integrals.

For complex $f_n$, apply step 2.1 separately to their real and imaginary parts, each dominated by $g$; their integral limits combine to $\int f_0$. To prove $L^1$ convergence, apply Fatou to the nonnegative functions $2g-|f_n-f_0|$, which converge to $2g$; it gives $2\int g\le2\int g-\limsup_n\int|f_n-f_0|$, so the latter limsup is zero. Therefore $\int|f_n-f_0|\to0$ as claimed.

citations.quote:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with a finite-valued slope map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.
Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$ of dimension $k\ge1$, let $\operatorname{aff}C=H$, and put $K=\overline{C}^{\,H}$. If $z\in\partial_H K$ (that is, $z\in K$ and every relative neighborhood of $z$ meets $H\setminus K$), then there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell$ on the translation space of $H$ such that $\ell(q-z)\le0$ for all $q\in C$. If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine dimension at most $d-2$, then every $z\in C$ has at least two distinct ambient supporting hyperplanes containing $\operatorname{aff}C$.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be closed and convex with nonempty interior, $d\ge1$, and let $x\in\partial K$. Suppose $K$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$. Choose its inward unit normal $n$, so $n\cdot(q-x)\ge0$ for every $q\in K$. Then for every $v$ with $n\cdot v>0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that $x+tv\in\operatorname{int}K$ for every $0<t<\delta$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be finite and convex, meaning $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for every $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$. For every $x_0\in U$, there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ and $L<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in V$. The same conclusion holds for finite concave functions by applying the result to $-f$.
Let $L\ge0$, $T>0$, and let $f:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous. If $f(t)\le L\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, then $f(t)=0$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: For fixed $x=(u_x,v_x)$, the vertical section $I_x:=\{u:(u,v_x)\in A_x\}$ is a relatively closed convex interval by [F1]. The support plane at $x$ confines it to one side of $u_x$. Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side.

The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant.

Let $u,w$ be two $C^1$ graph solutions of $Dq=-P_i(q,v)$ on a common open domain, and suppose $u(v_0)=w(v_0)$. Since $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz, choose a convex neighborhood of $(u(v_0),v_0)$ on which one Lipschitz constant $L$ works. Continuity of $u,w$ lets us choose a convex ball about $v_0$ whose closure lies in the common domain and whose two graph images stay in that neighborhood; take any $v$ in a smaller concentric ball. Put $d=v-v_0$ and $\gamma(t)=v_0+td$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F8], $r(t)=u(\gamma(t))-w(\gamma(t))$ is $C^1$ and
$r'(t)=[-P_i(u(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))+P_i(w(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))]\cdot d.$
The local Lipschitz bound for $P_i$ gives $|r'(t)|\le L\|d\||r(t)|$. The derivative is continuous, hence integrable by [F10]; [F9] gives $r(t)=\int_0^t r'(s)\,ds$; hence $h(t):=|r(t)|\le L\|d\|\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $h=0$. Thus $u=w$ near $v_0$. Along any polygonal path in the common open domain, the set of path parameters at which equality holds is closed by continuity and open by this local result; since the path interval is connected and the set is nonempty, equality holds along the whole path. Every open connected subset of Euclidean space is polygonally connected: points reachable from a fixed point by finitely many segments in small balls form a nonempty relatively open and relatively closed set. Therefore equality extends throughout each common connected domain.

The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Its endpoint $b$ toward that side then lies inside $\Gamma_i$; relative closedness puts $b$ in $I_x$, so the interval from $x$ to $b$ is a compact nondegenerate interval by [F7]. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. These intervals have nonempty total intersection: otherwise their open complements would cover the first compact interval, a finite subcover would do so by [F7], and nesting would make one interval empty. Their lengths tend to zero, so the intersection has a unique point $x_\infty$, still in the first interval contained in $\Gamma_i$. The midpoint recursion and this unique intersection require no selection from an arbitrary countable family. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side.

All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$.
Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$.

Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 4.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$.

For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$
Local Lipschitz continuity of $u_x$ and $P_i$ makes the difference between these linear bounds $O(\|v'-v\|^2)$. Thus $u_x$ is differentiable with derivative $-P_i(u_x(v),v)$, and that derivative is locally Lipschitz. Hence $u_x\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative.

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. The set of $v\in\rho_y$ where $v\in\rho_x$ and $u_y(v)=u_x(v)$ is nonempty, open by step 1.3, and closed by continuity and relative closedness of $\partial A_x$. Connectedness of $\rho_y$ makes it all of $\rho_y$. This shows $\rho_y\subseteq\rho_x$. The same argument, using relative closedness of $\partial A_y$, shows $\rho_y$ is relatively closed in connected $\rho_x$; it is relatively open because both projections are open. Hence $\rho_x=\rho_y$ and the boundary graphs agree. In particular $x\in\partial A_y$, so $y\prec x$; together with $y\in A_x$ and transitivity this gives $A_x=A_y$.
